title: Bertha Benz's Daring Drive
summary: One summer morning in 1888, Bertha Benz and her two teenage sons sneaked off in her husband's brand-new car and drove it all the way to Grandma's house, more than 100 kilometres away. Along the way she bought fuel at a pharmacy, fixed the car with a hatpin and a garter, and had a shoemaker mend the brakes. Her adventure showed the world that cars really could go places!

sections.heading: The Girl from Pforzheim Who Bet on a Dream
paragraphs: Every famous invention has a person standing just outside the spotlight, and for the automobile that person is Bertha Benz. She was born Cäcilie Bertha Ringer on 3 May 1849 in Pforzheim, a busy town on the northern edge of the Black Forest in the Grand Duchy of Baden, one of the small states that would soon join together to form Germany. Pforzheim was famous for its jewellery and watch workshops. Bertha was the third of nine children, so the Ringer house was a lively, crowded place.

Bertha was clever and curious about machines, but in her time a girl's choices were narrow. Universities in Baden did not accept women as students, so she could not study engineering even if she had wanted to. What she could do was choose whom to trust, and she chose a serious, stubborn young engineer named Karl Benz. You met him in Part 4: the railway driver's son from Karlsruhe who dreamed of a carriage that moved by itself.

In 1870, before they were even married, Bertha used part of her dowry (the money and property a bride's family gave when she married) to invest in Karl's struggling iron-construction business in Mannheim. It was a brave and risky choice. Karl's business partner turned out to be unreliable, money was always short, and creditors were often knocking at the door. Bertha and Karl married on 20 July 1872, and over the next years they had five children: Eugen (born 1873), Richard (1874), Clara (1876), Thilde (1882) and Ellen (1890).

Here is the unfair twist. Once Bertha married, the law of the time took away much of her power to act on her own in business. Her money was now treated as her husband's. When the Patent-Motorwagen was finished, Karl applied for German patent number 37435 in his own name alone. Bertha could not legally be named as an inventor or owner beside him, even though her dowry had kept the workshop alive through the hungry years. Historians today describe her not just as 'the inventor's wife' but as his investor and partner, and the story of August 1888 shows why.

sections.heading: Summer 1888: A Car Nobody Wanted
paragraphs: By the summer of 1888 Karl Benz had a problem that had nothing to do with engineering. He had a working car, but hardly anyone wanted to buy it. Since his first public drive on Mannheim's Ringstrasse in 1886, he had built improved versions: the Model II and then the Model III. Only a handful of Patent-Motorwagens had been made in total; one estimate is that about six existed by 1888, counting prototypes, and only around 25 were built in all between 1886 and 1893. A French bicycle maker named Émile Roger had bought one and become Benz's agent in Paris, but in Germany people mostly stared, laughed or worried that the noisy thing would scare their horses.

Part of the trouble was Karl himself. He was a perfectionist who preferred tinkering in the workshop to showing off. He would test his car on short trips around Mannheim, often at night or in quiet places, and then return to the workshop to improve it again. Nobody outside the family had seen a Motorwagen travel a really long way, so nobody knew whether it could. Would it break down after ten kilometres? Could it climb a hill? Where would you even get fuel for it?

Abroad, things were only a little better. Émile Roger had bought the first Benz car ever sold, in 1887, in what was really a semi-private deal, and before March 1888 he had sold another Motorwagen to a French engineer named Émile Levassor, a man you will meet again in Part 6. So a few people in Paris were paying attention. But one or two sales a year could not pay the wages of a workshop. Benz & Cie. still earned most of its money from stationary gas engines for factories, and Karl's business partners were reportedly not keen on spending money on the car.

The car Bertha took is usually described as a Model III (some historians think it was actually a Model II). It looked like a large tricycle built for two adults, with a small bench seat high up, one wheel in front for steering with a tiller (a lever, not a steering wheel) and two large wheels at the back. Behind the seat sat the single-cylinder engine and a big flywheel. Power went to the rear wheels through leather belts and chains. There was no fuel tank as we know it: the car carried only about 4.5 litres of fuel in its carburetor. There was no proper cooling radiator either. Instead the engine was cooled by evaporation: water around the cylinder simply boiled away as steam and had to be topped up again and again.

The brakes were wooden blocks pressed against the iron rims of the rear wheels by a hand lever, rather like the brakes on a farm cart. There was no roof, no windscreen and no lights. Early versions had only two gears, and the lower one was still not low enough for steep hills. In other words, the Model III was a brilliant machine for a smooth, flat street in Mannheim, and a very doubtful one for a real journey into the countryside. Bertha decided to find out which it was.

sections.heading: How to Drive a Car in 1888
paragraphs: Before we follow Bertha onto the road, imagine you are taking a driving lesson in a Motorwagen. Forget everything you know about cars. There is no key, no starter button, no pedals for speed, and no steering wheel. Instead, you climb up onto a padded bench, quite high above the road, with nothing in front of you but a small upright lever called a tiller. Pushing the tiller left or right turns the single front wheel, a bit like steering a boat with a rudder.

To start the engine, someone has to turn the big flywheel by hand. The flywheel is a heavy wheel that keeps spinning once it gets going, smoothing out the engine's jerky pushes. Inside the single cylinder, each turn of the flywheel helps draw in a mixture of air and fuel vapour from the carburetor. An electric spark, made by a battery and an induction coil, lights the mixture. Bang, and the piston is shoved along its cylinder. With luck, after a few heaves the engine catches and settles into a steady, thumping rhythm, and you are ready to go.

Now for the clever part. The engine is running, but the car is not moving yet. That is because the leather drive belt is sitting on a 'loose' pulley, a wheel that spins freely without driving anything. When you move a hand lever, the belt slides across onto a 'fixed' pulley that is connected through gears and chains to the rear wheels. The car lurches forward. This sliding belt does the job that a clutch does in a modern car: it connects and disconnects the engine from the wheels. To stop, you slide the belt back and pull the brake lever, which presses the wooden blocks against the rear wheels.

Top speed on a good road was around 16 kilometres per hour, about as fast as a fit person can run for a short time, or a horse at a steady trot. On rough tracks and hills it was much slower. It was also loud, smelly and bumpy, and it needed constant attention: watching the water, listening to the engine, checking the chains and belts. Driving a Motorwagen was less like driving a car today and more like nursing a temperamental machine across the countryside.

It is worth remembering one more thing. In 1888 Mannheim and Pforzheim were already connected by railway, so Bertha could have made the same journey much faster and more comfortably by train. That is exactly the point. She was not travelling because she needed to get to Pforzheim; she was travelling to prove that the car could get her there. The long, difficult road was the experiment.

sections.heading: Slipping Out at Dawn
paragraphs: The trip is usually dated to 5 August 1888. According to the family's account, Bertha did not tell Karl what she was planning. Very early in the morning, while he was still asleep (so the story goes), she and her two oldest sons, Eugen, who was 15, and Richard, who was 13 or 14 (accounts differ slightly), quietly pushed the Motorwagen out of the workshop so the noise would not wake him. Only when they were a safe distance from the house did they start the engine, which was done by heaving the heavy flywheel round by hand.

Officially, Bertha was going to visit her mother in Pforzheim, about 106 kilometres (roughly 65 miles) to the south. That was true, but it was not the whole truth. She wanted to show the world, and especially her worried, doubtful husband, that the car could make a real journey, and she wanted people to see it. A car rattling through a dozen towns would be far better advertising than one hidden in a Mannheim workshop. She also had no special permission to make such a long drive on public roads, so the journey carried a little risk of trouble with the authorities as well as with the machine.

Picture the scene. There are no road signs for cars, because there are no cars. There are no maps meant for drivers. Bertha follows the routes she knows: the roads and wagon tracks used by horse carts and coaches, dusty in summer and full of ruts and stones. The car bounces along on its wooden wheels with iron rims and no air-filled tyres, so every bump goes straight up through the seat. The engine chugs and clatters behind them. The boys take turns helping, and some retellings say Eugen took a turn at the tiller, though Bertha is the one remembered as the driver.

Their route led south from Mannheim to Heidelberg, the old university town with its famous ruined castle above the river Neckar, then on to Wiesloch, Bruchsal and Grötzingen near Karlsruhe, and finally up into the hills to Pforzheim. Farmers stopped working in the fields to stare. Children ran alongside. Some were curious, some were frightened, and horses shied at the strange clattering noise. For most of them, it was the first motor car they had ever seen.

sections.heading: The World's First Filling Station
paragraphs: The first big problem arrived quickly: fuel. The Motorwagen did not run on petrol from a pump, because petrol pumps did not exist. It burned ligroin, a light, quick-evaporating liquid made from petroleum and sold as a cleaning solvent, rather like the spirit people used to remove grease spots from clothes. Where could you buy a cleaning fluid in 1888? At the pharmacy, of course, alongside medicines, soaps and chemicals.

With her small supply running low, Bertha stopped in the town of Wiesloch, south of Heidelberg, and went into the Stadt-Apotheke, the town pharmacy. The pharmacist, Willi Ockel, sold her ligroin, and the Motorwagen was ready to roll again. Because of that purchase, the Wiesloch town pharmacy is proudly called the world's first filling station. It still stands, and a memorial in Wiesloch remembers Bertha's stop. Of course, nobody in the shop that day knew they were making history; to them she was simply a surprising customer who wanted rather a lot of cleaning fluid.

Fuel was not the only thing the car drank. Remember that the engine was cooled by letting water boil away. On a long, hot summer drive that meant the car needed water constantly. Whenever they could, Bertha and the boys refilled it at inns, wells, streams and even roadside ditches. A few years later, in 1894, a careful driver of a Benz car measured that it used up to about 150 litres of water for every 100 kilometres, compared with about 21 litres of fuel. That shows how thirsty these early cooling systems were. The family's journey was really a long chain of small stops: fuel here, water there, a quick check of the chains, then onward.

This is why Bertha's drive was such a good test. It was not only a test of the car; it was a test of whether ordinary towns could support a car at all. The answer was yes, with some creativity. Pharmacies could sell fuel, inns could supply water, and local craftsmen could make repairs. That is a small version of what would later become the whole network of filling stations, garages and mechanics that cars depend on today.

sections.heading: Hatpins, Garters and Leather: Fixing a Car with No Garages
paragraphs: Today, if a car breaks down, you call a mechanic or a breakdown truck. In 1888 there were no mechanics who had ever repaired a car, because there were hardly any cars to repair. If something went wrong, Bertha and the boys had to fix it themselves with whatever they had. The family's story of the trip is famous for three clever repairs. They have been told so many times that small details vary, but they fit everything we know about the car's weak points.

First, the fuel line became blocked. A tiny bit of dirt in a thin pipe was enough to starve the engine of fuel, and the car stopped. Bertha took the long hatpin from her hat, the sharp pin women used to hold their hats on, and poked it through the pipe until the blockage was cleared. Fuel flowed again and the engine came back to life.

Second, there was trouble with the ignition, the electrical system that made the spark to light the fuel. A wire had lost its insulation, the covering that stops electricity escaping where it should not go. Bertha used her garter, an elastic band worn to hold up a stocking, to wrap the bare wire and insulate it. It sounds funny, but it was exactly the right idea: cover the wire with something that does not conduct electricity.

Third, and most important for the future of cars, the brakes began to fail. The Model III's brakes were wooden blocks pressed against the wheel rims. On the long downhill stretches the wood was rubbed away fast. In one village Bertha found a shoemaker and asked him to nail pieces of leather onto the brake blocks. Leather gripped better and wore down more slowly than bare wood. Without knowing it, the shoemaker had made one of the first brake linings, the replaceable, hard-wearing layer that still sits on the brake pads and shoes of every car today, although modern linings are made from special tough materials rather than leather.

There were other problems too. A drive chain stretched and needed repair, and a blacksmith helped fix it. And then there were the hills. With only two gears, the little engine simply did not have enough pulling force to climb the steepest slopes with three people on board. On those hills Eugen and Richard jumped down and pushed, sometimes with Bertha steering and sometimes with all three heaving together. It must have been hot, dusty and exhausting work in the August sun, and it gave Bertha a very clear message to bring home: this car needs a lower gear.

sections.heading: Dusk in Pforzheim and a Telegram Home
paragraphs: The family had left Mannheim at dawn. Hour after hour they bumped south, stopping for fuel, water and repairs, pushing up hills and riding the brakes down them. Darkness was falling by the time the Motorwagen rattled into Pforzheim, and the car had no headlights. They arrived somewhat after dusk, tired and dusty but triumphant. Counting all the stops, the trip of about 106 kilometres had taken most of a long summer day, which works out at an average speed slower than a gently trotting horse. Still, nothing about the car had stopped them for good.

Bertha did one more important thing that evening: she sent a telegram to Karl in Mannheim to tell him they had arrived safely. A telegram was a short message sent as electric signals along wires and then delivered on paper, the fastest way to send news over long distances in 1888. We can only imagine Karl's feelings when he discovered his car, his wife and two of his sons were all missing, and then learned that they had driven it all the way to Pforzheim.

Bertha spent a few days with her mother, and the car was the talk of the town. Then the family drove home. For the return trip Bertha chose a different route, partly to avoid the steepest hills. The modern memorial route follows a northern path back through Bretten, Bruchsal, Hockenheim and Schwetzingen, partly along the plain of the river Rhine. Once again the Motorwagen made it, and once again people along the way saw a car with their own eyes for the very first time.

By the time they rolled back into Mannheim, Bertha, Eugen and Richard had driven roughly 200 kilometres in total. Nobody had done anything like it before in a car with an internal combustion engine. The machine that many people had laughed at had crossed a large part of Baden, climbed (with help) into the hills, found fuel in a pharmacy and survived repairs made with a hatpin, a garter and some leather.

sections.heading: Why One Road Trip Changed Everything
paragraphs: Bertha's journey is considered the first long-distance trip ever made by automobile. Be careful with what that means: it was not the first time a car had been driven, since Karl and others had already made short drives. It was the first time a car proved it could carry people a real distance, between two cities, over ordinary roads, with ordinary towns supplying what it needed. That was the question every possible buyer was asking, and Bertha answered it.

The trip also worked like a road test, the kind every carmaker still does today. Bertha came home with a list of practical improvements. The car needed an extra, lower gear for climbing hills, and Karl added one. The brakes needed proper linings, and later Benz cars had leather-covered brake blocks. Karl also enlarged the engine to give it more power. In a way, Bertha was not only the first long-distance driver but also one of the first test drivers and product testers in automotive history.

It mattered, too, that the driver was a woman. In 1888 many people assumed that machines were a man's business, and that a woman could hardly be trusted with one. Bertha drove the car, navigated with no maps, bought fuel, organised repairs and solved breakdowns with her own hands and ideas, all while looking after two teenagers. Her drive has become a symbol of women's place in the history of technology. It was retold in a German television film, Carl & Bertha, in 2011, and Mercedes-Benz used the story in an advertisement for International Women's Day in 2019. More than 130 years later, it still makes a great adventure story because it really was one.

Then there was publicity. News of the woman who drove a horseless carriage from Mannheim to Pforzheim spread from town to town. The next year, 1889, the Model III was shown at the great World's Fair in Paris, the same fair that opened the Eiffel Tower, though sales there were disappointing. Benz's French agent, Émile Roger, proved much better at selling than Karl was, and slowly orders grew. In 1894 Benz launched the cheaper, lighter Velo, which sold more than 1,200 cars by 1902. Benz & Cie. grew from about 50 workers in 1889 to 430 in 1899, when it built 572 vehicles and was the largest car company in the world.

Bertha lived to see the car go from a laughed-at oddity to an everyday machine. In 1906 the family moved to the small town of Ladenburg near Mannheim, where Karl died in 1929. Bertha lived on there quietly. On her 95th birthday, 3 May 1944, the Technical University of Karlsruhe made her an honorary senator, and she died two days later, on 5 May 1944. By then millions of cars were on the roads of the world.

Today her journey is remembered on the ground. In 2008 the Bertha Benz Memorial Route was approved as a signposted tourist route, and it is part of the European Route of Industrial Heritage. Its signs lead drivers about 104 kilometres from Mannheim through Heidelberg and Wiesloch to Pforzheim, and about 90 kilometres back by the northern route, roughly 194 kilometres in all. Since 2011 a Bertha Benz Challenge for clean, modern vehicles has been held along the route. In 2016 Bertha was inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame in the United States, 32 years after Karl.

News of her drive spread, and one question hung in the air: if a car could cross Baden, what else could it do? Meanwhile, only about 100 kilometres away in Cannstatt, near Stuttgart, two other German engineers had been working in a garden workshop on engines and vehicles of their own. Their names were Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, and they were in a race that Karl Benz did not even know he was running.

deepDive: Historians treat Bertha Benz's 1888 drive as a turning point, but they are careful about what it proves. It was not the first time a car moved under its own power, and it was not a race or an official trial. Its importance is that it was the first documented long-distance journey by a car with an internal combustion engine, made on ordinary roads between two cities, about 104 to 106 kilometres each way. Much of what we know about the details, such as the hatpin, the garter and the exact moment of departure, comes from family accounts told and retold in later years. That is why careful writers describe the repairs as 'the family's story'. They are entirely believable, because they match the Motorwagen's known weak points: thin fuel lines, exposed ignition wiring, and wooden brake blocks that wore away on long descents. The numbers tell their own tale. The car carried only about 4.5 litres of fuel in its carburetor, so it had to be refuelled on the way, and its evaporative cooling meant water was a bigger problem than fuel: a Benz car measured in 1894 used up to about 150 litres of water per 100 kilometres against about 21 litres of fuel. Closed cooling systems with radiators, developed largely through Wilhelm Maybach's patents from 1897 onward, eventually solved this. Bertha's legal position is another topic historians discuss. Her dowry money funded Karl's business from 1870, yet as a married woman in the German states of the time she could not be named on the 1886 patent, and her contribution was long described in terms of loyalty rather than investment. Many modern writers now describe her as Karl's investor and partner, not just his supporter. Finally, the drive was also a piece of marketing. Benz & Cie. sold very few cars before 1890, but within a decade it was building hundreds a year (572 in 1899) and was the world's largest carmaker. The drive alone did not cause that growth, but it helped turn a curiosity into a product people could imagine using.
funFact: The pharmacy in Wiesloch where Bertha Benz bought her fuel in 1888 is still known today as the world's first filling station.
